question: How can state-value functions be estimated from on-policy experience when the value function is a parameterized function of a weight vector instead of a table?
contributions: Frames each RL update s -> u as a supervised training example
Defines the mean square value error VE and the on-policy distribution
Derives gradient Monte Carlo and semi-gradient TD(0) / n-step TD, with linear-case convergence to the TD fixed point and its error bound
Surveys feature constructions (polynomial, Fourier, coarse and tile coding, RBF), step-size heuristics, ANNs, LSTD, memory-based and kernel methods, interest and emphasis

limits: Covers prediction only (fixed policy, on-policy); control with function approximation is Chapter 10, off-policy divergence is Chapter 11.
VE may not be the right objective for finding a better policy (Sec 9.2).
Convergence theory is mostly limited to tabular and linear approximation; deep ANN success is not backed by it (Sec 9.7).
Backprop in deep ANNs is said to work poorly without extra techniques (dropout, batch norm, residual connections, layer-wise pretraining); this reflects the 2018 edition and has dated.
Examples are single toy tasks (1000-state random walk); few hyperparameters are given and no seeds beyond the run counts in captions.
practices: Treat each RL update s -> u as a supervised training example, then use any online-capable function approximator (Sec 9.1).
Use a semi-gradient TD method when you need online, continual learning and faster learning; accept it is not a true gradient method (Sec 9.3).
Do not use plain polynomial features for online RL; prefer Fourier basis or tile coding (Sec 9.5.2, 9.12).
Tile coding: set alpha = 1/(tau*n) for n tilings, offset tilings asymmetrically, use hashing to cut memory (Sec 9.5.4).
Set step size by alpha = (tau E[x^T x])^-1 instead of 1/t, which is wrong for TD and function approximation (Sec 9.6).
Use interest and emphasis when only some states matter (Sec 9.11).
For deep ANNs, use dropout, batch normalization, residual connections or convolutional structure (Sec 9.7).

terms.definition: Bootstrapping methods take into account the effect of changing the weight vector on the estimate but ignore its effect on the target; they include only a part of the gradient.
VE(w) = sum_s mu(s)[v_pi(s) - vhat(s,w)]^2, where mu is the on-policy distribution.
The fraction of time spent in each state while following pi; in continuing tasks the stationary distribution under pi.
w_TD = A^-1 b, with A = E[x_t (x_t - gamma x_{t+1})^T] and b = E[R_{t+1} x_t].
A form of coarse coding where receptive fields are grouped into offset partitions (tilings) of the state space, so exactly one tile per tiling is active.
Least-Squares TD: estimates A and b from data and solves for the TD fixed point directly, O(d^2) per step.
Interest I_t is a non-negative measure of how much we care about valuing the state at t; emphasis M_t = I_t + gamma^n M_{t-n} scales the update.
States are grouped, with one estimated value (one weight) per group; a special case of SGD where the gradient is 1 for the group's component and 0 elsewhere.
